3.0.s.en: 1. Preparing for the coming of the Messiah:

3.0.0.en: 1 "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts."

3.0.1.en: In contempt the wicked were asking: "Where is the God of judgment?" (Mal 2:17). The answer came at once: He will come in the fullness of time, and this was now at the doors.

3.0.2.en: Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me.

3.0.3.en: And the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in.

3.0.4.en: Behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts. [1]

3.0.5.en: The Lord refers to St. John the Baptist, whom He sends before Him to prepare the way for Him by proclaiming repentance, offering the baptism of repentance, and bearing witness to the Lord as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

3.0.6.en: He calls St. John His messenger (angel). Here many of the Fathers of the Church stand in amazement before God's surpassing love for man, for He desires to call every person His own messenger (angel). He is enamored of man and wants to raise him to the highest heavenly level.

3.0.7.en: God prepared humanity for His coming since the fall of Adam and Eve, when He gave them the promise: "I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel" (Gen 3:15). Then came the fathers and the prophets presenting types and prophecies about His coming, and finally God sends John the Baptist as a messenger (angel) to prepare the way for the promised Messiah, and God called him "my messenger" [1]. He comes to proclaim the divine message that he received from heaven and not from men. The Holy Bible was sealed with this promise, and the opening of the Gospel of our teacher the Apostle Mark, being the first of the Gospels to be written, bears witness to the fulfillment of this promise (Mk 1:12).

3.0.8.en: St. John the Baptist came to prepare the way before the Lord Christ by proclaiming repentance and offering the baptism of repentance. He came to declare to them that their salvation does not lie in their physical descent from Abraham the father of the fathers, but in the coming of Him whose coming Abraham hoped for.

3.0.9.en: This prophecy came perfectly clear, and it was fulfilled in the person of St. John the Baptist, who bore witness to Jesus Christ that He is "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29). For this reason the Jews tried to offer various interpretations of this text; some claimed that Malachi is speaking of himself as the messenger (angel) of the Lord, and others claimed that it refers to the angel of death who leads the wicked to cast them into the fire of Gehenna.

3.0.10.en: The prophet affirms that the Messiah, the Lord, comes suddenly to His temple, He whom the pious, those who fear the Lord, have sought since the days of Adam and Eve. They await Him with great joy, and as the Evangelist says, they were "waiting for the consolation of Israel" (Lk 2:25), and for redemption in Israel (Lk 2:38), for He is "the desire of all nations" (Hag 2:7). All find in Him the delight of their hearts.

3.0.11.en: "He shall suddenly come." His coming has drawn near, so we no longer wait for Him from afar as the patriarchs did, and the prophets after them, but the Messiah has come to be at the doors. Perhaps by "suddenly" he means that He will come at a time when many did not expect His coming, despite the clarity of the prophecies and the fixing of the date of His coming as given in the book of Daniel. Truly, at His birth the priests affirmed that He is born in Bethlehem Ephratah, but to them He came suddenly, since they were not prepared for His coming, although they knew this with their minds.

3.0.12.en: "To his temple": He came to the Temple in Jerusalem and cleansed it more than once of the sellers of doves and the moneychangers. He did this with authority, because it is His temple and His house. At the age of twelve He stood in the Temple in the midst of the teachers, drawing their hearts by His authority, for He was about His Father's business (Lk 2:49). And when He entered Jerusalem in the last week He went to the Temple directly (Mt 21:12). There the blind and the lame came to Him seeking healing (Mt 21:14). There He preached, debated, and performed signs and miracles.

3.0.13.en: Although He came to establish a new temple in the hearts of His believers, He honored the Temple in Jerusalem, demanding of us respect for the house of God.

3.0.14.en: "Behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts," for the One who speaks is faithful in His promises and able to fulfill them; He has come and has not delayed.

3.0.15.en: * "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John" (Jn 1:6)... He was called "a messenger" (Mal 3:1), because the privilege of a messenger is that he says nothing of his own.

3.0.16.en: * Jesus spoke about John's clothing, his imprisonment, and his role in prophecy; by saying this He showed that he was greater than a prophet. What else does Jesus mean by his being greater? That he was very near to the One who was coming. He says: "Behold, I send my messenger before thy face," meaning his nearness to the Messiah. For as with kings, the one who rides beside the chariot is more famous than the rest, so it was with John, who appears in turn to be near to the very coming.

3.0.17.en: St. John Chrysostom * John is greater than the other prophets for the following reason: the other prophets prophesied about John that he was coming, but John pointed with his finger that He had truly come, saying: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29). He did not merely reach the rank of a prophet, but the Baptist, by baptizing his Lord, was exalted. By this he fulfilled the prophecy of Malachi, who prophesied about a messenger (angel). John belonged to the order of the angels, not by nature, but because of the importance of his mission. It means that he is the messenger who announces the coming of the Lord.

3.0.18.en: St. Jerome * By the word "angels" (Gal 3:19) he means the messengers of God, that is, Moses, the son of Nun, and other prophets up to John the Baptist.

3.0.19.en: Father Ambrosiaster * In this text he foretells to us both comings of Christ, the first and the second. The first, where he says: "The Lord shall suddenly come to his temple." This refers to the body of Christ, of which He Himself said in the Gospel: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (Jn 2:19). And His second coming he prophesied in these words: "But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth?"

3.0.20.en: * Men are called angels, for the Apostle says of himself: "Ye received me as an angel of God" (Gal 4:14). And it is said of John the Baptist: "Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee" (Mt 11:10). Therefore at His coming with all His angels (Mt 25:31), His saints will also be with Him.

3.1.0.en: 2 But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap: 3 And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.

3.1.1.en: The holy Lord comes to establish from humanity His holy temple. With His marvelous love for man and His esteem for him, and though He counts them as heavenly gold or silver, He does not accept that there be in him any dross or defilement. He desires to clothe him with His divine righteousness, so that his heart becomes a holy temple, and God smells in every worship or offering a sweet savor, the object of His divine delight.

3.1.2.en: But who may abide the day of his coming?

3.1.3.en: And who shall stand when he appeareth?

3.1.4.en: For he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap. [2]

3.1.5.en: Although He came incarnate in humility, to meet all classes, even the slaves who were despised at that time, yet "who may abide the day of his coming?" "Who shall stand when he appeareth?" He came not to judge but to save the world, and yet He was the One with authority before whom the Jewish leaders trembled.

3.1.6.en: This is about His first coming to save; what will it be at His last coming to judge? The believers see Him with eyes like doves, while the wicked look at Him with eyes burning with fire!

3.1.7.en: The Lord Christ came like the refiner's fire, like the fullers' soap (lye) that purifies and cleans cloths of the filth that clings to them. He came to send fire on the earth (Lk 12:49-50).

3.1.8.en: * Christ Himself, who did all this, will afterward stand before us as our Judge. Certainly the prophets did not pass over this, but prophesied about Him. Some saw Him in the very form in which He will be when He stands before us, and some prophesied only through words. Daniel was among the barbarians and the Babylonians when he saw Christ coming on the clouds. Listen to his words: "I saw, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him" (cf. Dan 7:13-14). He pointed to the judgment of God and His verdict, saying: The thrones were set up, the books were opened. A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him. Thousands of thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him (Dan 7:9-10). Daniel did not declare this only, but showed the honor that the righteous receive when he said: "Judgment was given to the saints of the most High; and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom" (Dan 7:22). This judgment will come through fire. Malachi said: "He is coming (like the fire of a refining furnace), like fullers' soap." Then the righteous will enjoy great honor. And Daniel speaks of the resurrection where he says: "Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake" (Dan 12:12).

3.1.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * When we fell, the horn of salvation was raised up for us (Lk 1:69), and the chief cornerstone (Isa 28:16), who binds us to Himself and to one another, was laid at the right time, or the fire (Mal 3:2-3) arose which purifies our debased and evil matters (1 Cor 3:13-15).

3.1.10.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus One of the Fathers of the Church says: [It is not presumptuous that John is called an angel though he is a man, because of his power and worthiness, for he is more glorious than if he were an angel in name or in nature. For an angel is called an angel because of his nature as an angel rather than because he has qualified for it. But it is a miraculous thing that a man, while in his human nature, passes over into angelic holiness and receives the grace of God which is not according to nature].

3.1.11.en: And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver:

3.2.0.en: And he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness. [3]

3.2.1.en: "He shall sit as a refiner," for He purifies humanity by His Gospel to establish from it a holy Church without blemish. He removes the dross from her, so she becomes pure gold refined by fire. The Apostle Paul says: "Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish" (Eph 5:25-27). And also: "Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works..." (Titus 2:14).

3.2.2.en: "He shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver." It is as though the Lord Christ purifies those who accepted to consecrate their lives to Him, for His praise and service and the offering of their hearts as living sacrifices, so that they become the spiritual sons of Levi of the New Testament.

3.2.3.en: Although the Lord Christ chose the disciples and the Apostles and gave them the gift of the priesthood, and their successors accordingly came to receive the same gift, yet there is a general priesthood that the believer receives in the sacrament of Baptism. Through it the believer offers his prayers, fasts, gifts, and service as spiritual offerings acceptable to God. St. John says in the name of the whole Church: "[He] hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father" (Rev 1:6).

3.2.4.en: The Lord Christ purifies His believers by His fiery Holy Spirit "through manifold temptations: that the trial of your faith... might be found unto praise and honour and glory" (1 Pet 1:6-7).

3.2.5.en: By the work of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the believers, "the offering up of the Gentiles... [is] acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost" (Rom 15:16). Thus they fulfill the words of the psalmist: "Offer the sacrifices of righteousness" (Ps 4:5). And the words of the Apostle Paul: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service" (Rom 12:1).

3.2.6.en: * Remove the defilement of their blasphemy that has come upon them, and cleanse with the breaths of holy purification the souls buried in the foul mire, so that dens of robbers may be turned into houses of prayer.

3.2.7.en: * If they know nothing of the mysteries and visions, but have formed their judgments only on their own present interests... their stupidity in understanding prophecy is great, and their envy in human affairs is great. Such stupidity and envy must be uprooted from our minds. It befits a man to be more fervent than fire in order to stand against such a company. This is the reason for which Christ said: "I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?" (Lk 12:49) and for this the Spirit appeared in (the form of) fire.

3.2.8.en: St. John Chrysostom * "He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire" (Mt 3:11)... The blessed Baptist added to the word "Spirit" the expression that carries the sense of action: "and with fire." This does not mean that we are baptized by Christ with fire, but that through the reference to fire the life-giving power of the Spirit is granted to us.

3.3.s.en: 3. He changes them and is not changed:

3.3.0.en: 4 Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the LORD, as in the days of old, and as in former years. 5 "And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts. 6 For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.

3.3.1.en: Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the LORD, as in the days of old, and as in former years. [4]

3.3.2.en: In the first chapter he spoke of their unclean offerings upon His altar (Mal 1:7); here, as he speaks of the coming of the Messiah and the believers' enjoyment of His righteousness, he says: "The offering of Judah and Jerusalem [shall] be pleasant unto the LORD" [4].

3.3.3.en: He speaks here of the new offering through the Cross, and the sacrifice of the Eucharist, which is the delight of the Father and not hateful to the Lord.

3.3.4.en: "As in the days of old, and as in former years": here he takes their memory back to the offering of Abel which God accepted, and the sacrifice of Noah after the Flood which God smelled as a sweet savor, and the sacrifice of Aaron when He sent down fire from heaven, and also the sacrifice of Elijah, and so on. So through the Cross the Lord makes us accepted in Him and beloved (Eph 1:6), and He delights in us and in what we offer to Him of what He gave us. The Apostle says of his ministry among the Gentiles with the Gospel of salvation: "That the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost" (Rom 15:16). The Apostle also asks us to offer a sacrifice acceptable to God through our union with the sacrifice of the Cross: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service" (Rom 12:1).

3.3.5.en: * How can the person who is conformed to this world, who has not been transformed by the renewing of his mind, and has not delighted in the newness of this life, but instead follows the life according to the old man, obey the Apostle, who commands you to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God? How can you, being a priest of God and anointed for this very purpose, offer an offering to God, not an offering entirely foreign to you or deceptive, as consisting of what is outside you, but one that truly seeks an offering which is yours, containing what is within you, the inner man in you, who helps you to be perfect and without blemish according to the word of the Lamb, having in him no wrath or blemish (Rom 8:9-11; 1 Cor 3:16-17; 2 Cor 13:5; Col 1:27)? How can you place these offerings before God if you do not listen to the Law that forbids any unholy man to be a priest?

3.3.6.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * The Gentiles were offered to God as an acceptable sacrifice when they believed in Christ and were sanctified by the Gospel.

3.3.7.en: St. Augustine And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages,

3.4.0.en: The widow, and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts. [5]

3.4.1.en: God, who has compassion on humanity as on His children, and receives them as His delight, and smells their gifts, from what He gave them, as a sweet savor of delight through the Cross, draws near to them to judge those who refuse to respond to His love and defy divine justice.

3.4.2.en: A. His witness by His Cross against the sorcerers: By His Cross He is a witness against the sorcerers who do not accept divine love, but trust in the power of their father the devil. At the close of the Holy Bible the Lord Himself warns against sorcery, and counts "sorcerers" among the groups whose portion is the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone, which is the second death, eternal (Rev 21:8).

3.4.3.en: B. His witness by His Cross against the adulterers who wallow in lusts. In the book of Isaiah the Lord rebukes the perverse people: "But draw near hither, ye sons of the sorceress, the seed of the adulterer and the whore" (Isa 57:3). And in Hosea: "Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband: let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts" (Hos 2:2). "They are all adulterers, as an oven heated by the baker" (Hos 7:4).

3.4.4.en: * At the beginning of the prophecy he gave the city the name "harlot." "How is the faithful city become an harlot!" (cf. Isa 1:21). Thus he accuses them of adultery, not only by their breaking the sanctity of marriage, but also by breaking the commandments; while they seemed to be near to God, they were secretly slaves to the demons, and this in fact is flagrant adultery.

3.4.5.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * She does not keep faithfulness in love toward me, but rather has betrayed intimacy and made light of the purity of union with me. And she has no desire to have the fruits of my will.

3.4.6.en: St. Cyril the Great C. His witness by His Cross against false swearers: Those who make light of the sanctity of God's name, and bear false witness. The Lord says in the prophet Zechariah: "It shall enter into the house of the thief, and into the house of him that sweareth falsely by my name: and it shall remain in the midst of his house, and shall consume it with the timber thereof and the stones thereof" (Hos 5:4).

3.4.7.en: D. His witness against those who wrong their brethren: They defraud the workers of their wages, crush the widow and the fatherless, and show no mercy to the stranger, depriving him of his rights because he does not know the law of the land. The Lord counted every action against these groups as a deprivation of the fear of the Lord and reverence for Him. The psalmist says of the wicked man: "There is no fear of God before his eyes" (Ps 36:1). God often warns us against practicing this injustice, counting that it is directed against Himself personally, and against His commandment. "Oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor" (Zech 7:10). "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child. If thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath shall wax hot, and I will kill you with the sword" (Ex 22:22-24). "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world" (Jas 1:27).

3.4.8.en: * Those who have no protection are the more exposed to being victims of tyranny. The humbler the victim, the more the oppressor is counted as one who resists God.

3.4.9.en: St. Jerome St. Jerome sees in the widow the soul that has lost God as its heavenly Bridegroom, and in the fatherless the soul deprived of God's fatherhood, and in the stranger the soul that has no place in which to rest, that is, in the divine embrace, and the hireling is the one who is occupied with material things rather than eternal things. It befits us to care for such souls, and not to make light of their salvation, so that they may enjoy fellowship with God, and the sweetness of salvation, and the fellowship of eternal glory.

3.5.0.en: For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed. [6]

3.5.1.en: God shows His longsuffering toward them. Their fathers had rebelled against Him and His servants since their beginning as a nation in Egypt, where the Jews said to Moses: "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?" (Ex 2:14); and after the Exodus, where the people murmured again and again against Moses and Aaron, and worshiped the golden calf. And even after entering the Promised Land, where they asked for themselves a king like all the nations (1 Sam 8:5), and the Lord said to Samuel the prophet: "They have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them" (1 Sam 8:7). Often they disobeyed the commandment, worshiped idols, and committed abominations. He says: "Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them"]7[. He reveals to them that instead of returning to Him they have filled up the cup of their fathers' evil. As Ezra says: "Since the days of our fathers have we been in a great trespass unto this day" (Ezra 9:7).

3.5.2.en: He did not leave them in bewilderment, but offered them the remedy, their return to Him, for He alone is the secret of their healing from their incurable diseases. Repentance is not merely a turning back from sin; what is positive in it is the return to God and their constant preoccupation with Him.

3.5.3.en: Unable to perceive the truth of their depths they said: "Wherein shall we return?" They thought, while in their evil and their treachery against God and their weak brethren, that they were with God, and that He dwelt in their midst merely because of their care for Jerusalem and the presence of the Temple in it.

3.5.4.en: By saying "Wherein shall we return?" they declare what is in their hearts of murmuring against the true prophets, for they count them as those who love rebuke and demand things that are not their right, and who stir up their consciences without real cause. So in arrogance they say: Wherein shall we return? Or what are the sins that you attribute against us?

3.5.5.en: As He warns those who have no fear of the Lord and who mistreat their brethren, especially the weak, the poor, and the strangers, He assures them that His warning is irrevocable unless they move toward His mercy by turning back from what they are in, and clinging to the Lord Himself. By saying "For I am the LORD, I change not," He assures them that not one word of His falls to the ground. He does not appease sin, and does not accept fellowship with darkness. If in His longsuffering He bore with His people so that they were not consumed, it is only because He awaits their return to Him by repentance. He is faithful in His love and in His divine promises. He is "not a man, that he should lie" (Num 23:19).

3.5.6.en: As the prophet Jeremiah says: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not" (Lam 3:22-23).

3.5.7.en: The reply of Origen the Scholar to Celsus, who attacked Christianity as well as Judaism and claimed that the doctrine of the Incarnation makes God, by His condescension, subject to change from good to evil, from virtue to vice, from happiness to misery, and from what is better to what is worse. He says: [While continuing unchanged in His essence, He came down to human affairs by the economy of His providence. We show that the Holy Scripture presents God as unchangeable by saying: "Thou art the same" (Ps 102:27) and "I change not." Whereas the gods of Epicurus, being composed of atoms, are subject to dissolution as long as their being is so, and they seek, indeed drive out, the atoms that contain elements of destruction. Even the god of the Stoics, being material, at one time has his whole substance consisting of the primary ruling element, when the world is consumed by fire. At another time, when things are reorganized, he becomes partly material. Even the Stoics were unable to grasp naturally the idea of God in a distinctive way, as a being entirely incorruptible, simple, and indivisible.

3.5.8.en: * Hear God saying: "I am he, I am he, I change not." He remains always constant and unchanging in His being, and those who are formed by the Gospel, and who have been changed by His commandments as far as they are able, will not turn aside from that in which they live through time. For this reason Paul also warns the people: "Be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God" (Rom 12:2).

3.5.9.en: St. Severus of Antioch * How can he be subject to change and alteration who says: "I am in the Father, and the Father in me" (Jn 14:10), and "I and my Father are one" (Jn 10:30), and by the prophet: "I am the LORD, I change not" (Mal 3:6)...? When He became man He did not change, but as the Apostle says: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 13:8).

3.5.10.en: Pope Alexander of Alexandria * God remains always as He is, and does not stand in need of progress, He who is always as He is, from Himself and to Himself.

3.5.11.en: St. Hilary of Poitiers * The creature is changed by the Creator as He pleases, for it is changeable and obeys the nod of Him who created it. But the Creator's nature is constant and unchangeable, therefore the prophet says of the nature of the Creator: [He is the maker of all things and the one who changes them] (cf. Amos 5:8) LXX. And of the divine Word the great David says: "Thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end" (Ps 102:27). Again God Himself says of Himself: "I am the LORD, I change not" (Mal 3:6).

3.5.12.en: * If by nature He is higher than change and alteration, then He does not pass from being incapable of death to being mortal, nor from being incapable of suffering to feeling suffering, for if this were possible there would have been no need for Him to take our nature.

3.5.13.en: Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * We need what the Apostle says: "And be renewed in the spirit of your mind" (Eph 4:23), and spiritual progress, for "forgetting those things which are behind" (Phil 3:13). If a person neglects to do so, the inevitable result is relapse and retreat from bad to worse.

3.5.14.en: The mind cannot remain in one state. Just as a man who rows strongly tries to resist with his boat against the strong storm, forcing his way through the current by the strength of his arms, and so presses on to what is ahead, but if he relaxes his hands, his boat turns quickly under the force of the storm, so our failure becomes clear if we gain nothing more. For without doubt we fall back when we are not advancing forward.

3.5.15.en: And as I said, the human mind cannot remain as it is, for no saint can reach the heights of all the virtues as long as he remains in the flesh, if he remains unchanged. Either he adds something or loses something. We confess that God alone is unchangeable, so the blessed prophet prays to Him saying: "But thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail" (Heb 1:12). And God says of Himself: "I am the LORD, I change not" (Mal 3:6). For He alone is by nature always good and wholly good, and nothing can be added to Him or taken from Him.

3.5.16.en: Therefore we must submit to the demands of virtue with great care and eagerness, and occupy ourselves with its work, because, as we said, the mind cannot remain in one state, that is, it cannot remain without its good qualities being increased or decreased. Failure to acquire new qualities means that there is a loss. And when the desire for progress ceases, there is danger of falling back.

3.5.17.en: Father Theodore * The Savior Himself says: "Behold, here am I, I change not" (Mal 3:6), while Paul writes: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 13:8), yet in the flesh He was circumcised, and carried, and ate and drank, and was troubled, and was hanged on a tree and suffered, and in Him was the Word of God, who is not subject to immaterial suffering.

3.5.18.en: * If (the Arians) slander thus by ascribing change to the Word, let them learn how great is the danger in their thought, for "the tree is known by his fruit" (Mt 12:23). And for this also: "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (Jn 14:9). And for this also the knowledge of the Son is also the knowledge of the Father. Therefore the unchanging image of God must be constant and unchanging, for "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 12:8). And David says singing of Him: "Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands: They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; and as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail" (Ps 102:26-28; Heb 12:10-12). And the Lord Himself says of Himself by the prophet: "See now that I, even I, am he" (Deut 32:39), and also: "I change not" (Mal 3:6). And perhaps someone will say that the Father is meant here. But it is fitting that this be said of the Son also. Especially since when He becomes man, He shows His person as it is, and shows His unchangeableness, for the sake of those who imagine that since He took a body, He has changed and become another... The nature of all creatures and all beings is changeable and alterable, and by excluding the Son from them, (Scripture) shows concerning Him by saying: "Thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail" (Heb 1:12). He (the Son) does not alter and does not change. And this is rightly natural. For created things, since they arose from nothing, and since they were not before they were created, therefore have a changeable nature, since in general they were created from nothing. But the Son is from the Father and is of the same essence as the Father, therefore it is not right for anyone to say that from the essence of the Unchangeable is born a changeable word, and a wisdom subject to alteration.

3.5.19.en: * Aaron had successors, and in general the men of the priesthood according to the Law take the place of their predecessors in time or because of death. But the Lord has "an unchangeable priesthood" (cf. Heb 7:24). He has become a faithful high priest abiding forever, and He became faithful according to the promise, so as to answer those who draw near to Him and not deceive them. And this you can learn from: "Let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator" (1 Pet 4:19), for He is faithful and unchangeable, but is constant forever, and He gives those things which He promised.

3.6.s.en: 4. Returning to the LORD of hosts:

3.6.0.en: 7 "Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. But ye said, Wherein shall we return? 8 Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings. 9 Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation. 10 Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it. 11 And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field, saith the LORD of hosts. 12 And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the LORD of hosts.

3.6.1.en: Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them.

3.6.2.en: Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts.

3.6.3.en: But ye said, Wherein shall we return? [7]

3.6.4.en: The Jews were occupied with offerings and sacrifices and their abundance, without caring for purity of heart and the practice of brotherly love, especially toward the needy. Therefore He declares to them that returning to Him with a living, practical faith must be realized through His poor brethren, "the brethren of the Lord," and as the beloved St. John says: "For he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" (1 Jn 4:20).

3.6.5.en: * While (the wicked man) angers God by his many and continual transgressions, God is longsuffering toward him, and in His longsuffering awaits the day of judgment, so that all may make up their minds (to repent)... He prefers to be longsuffering toward him for a long time, bearing with him in mercy, postponing (his punishment),... awaiting his return to Him, just as God Himself counsels us, saying: "For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye" (Ezek 18:32). Again: "Return unto me, saith the LORD of hosts" (cf. Mal 3:7).

3.6.6.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr * Seek the Lord, O sinners, and be strengthened in your thoughts because of hope. Seek His face by repentance at all times (Ps 105:3), and you will be sanctified by the holiness of His presence, and cleansed from your iniquities (Ezek 36:25). Hasten to the Lord, O sinners, for He blots out iniquity and removes sins. For He has sworn: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezek 33:11), but that the sinner repent and live. [I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious and disobedient people] (cf. Isa 65:2). "Why will ye die, O house of Israel?" (Ps 33:11). "Return unto me, and I will return unto you" (Mal 3:7).

3.6.7.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * Thou hadst a whore's forehead, thou refusedst to be ashamed (Jer 3:3). Return, O wretched one, to the Lord, and He will return to you [7]. Repent, and He will repent of the evil (the chastisement) which He was about to bring upon you.

3.6.8.en: St. Jerome Will a man rob God?

3.6.10.en: But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee?

3.7.1.en: The Lord Himself answers their question: "Ye have robbed me"] 8[This is a new accusation directed by the Lord Himself against the people through the prophet.

3.7.2.en: The first accusation: the priests' contempt for the name of the Lord (Mal 1:6).

3.7.3.en: The second accusation: they offer polluted bread upon the altar of the Lord (Mal 1:7).

3.7.4.en: The third accusation: they caused many to stumble at the Law, they corrupted the covenant of God (Mal 3:8).

3.7.5.en: The fourth accusation: treachery and the doing of an abomination in Israel and in Jerusalem (Mal 3:11).

3.7.6.en: The fifth accusation: they wearied the Lord with their words (Mal 3:17).

3.7.7.en: The sixth accusation: from the days of their fathers they turned aside from His ordinances and did not keep them (Mal 3:7).

3.7.8.en: The seventh accusation: they robbed the Lord (Mal 3:8).

3.7.9.en: The eighth accusation: their words have been stout against the Lord (Mal 3:13).

3.7.10.en: Here the seventh accusation is presented, which is an accusation of robbing the Lord by force, and taking away His rights over them. How can a weak creature rob God, who owns the world and everything, the Almighty? Does he imagine that he robs Him secretly without His knowledge or without His ability to resist? It is folly for a man to commit such a crime against God.

3.7.11.en: "But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee?" In boldness they justify themselves and ask God for proof that they committed this crime.

3.7.12.en: They robbed Him of the tithes of what He gave them freely, and of what they had vowed, and of the offerings prescribed in the Law. And by this they committed a crime against the whole nation, since the poor, the needy, and the destitute find no share for themselves in the house of the Lord. Moreover, since they acted stingily toward the house of God, the curse came upon the land, and the nation lost many of the good things and divine gifts because of this curse. Famines and plagues came, and nature rose up against man!

3.7.13.en: He had already chastened them with the same chastening when they were concerned with building their own houses and ignored the building of the house of the Lord (Hag 1:10-11), and now He repeats the chastening because they did not provide for the needs of the service in the Temple.

3.8.0.en: Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation. [9]

3.9.0.en: Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it. [10]

3.9.1.en: He gives them sincere advice so that they may experience in practice how generous giving opens before them the windows of heaven. He refers to the divine gifts as though from heaven, from where man did not expect, flowing upon him suddenly without expectation.

3.9.2.en: God in His love and generosity does not stop at reconciliation with the man who returns to Him, but pours out on him more than he can imagine!

3.10.0.en: And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field, saith the LORD of hosts. [11]

3.10.1.en: God removes from them the plague of "locusts" and the insects that ruin the fields, so that they no longer find a spoiled vine in their fields.

3.11.0.en: And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the LORD of hosts. [12]

3.11.1.en: Along with material gifts they receive esteem and respect from all the nations, as the peoples sense the Lord's delight in them, and call them blessed after they had become the object of the peoples' mockery because of their sins; even their land becomes a "delightsome land." As the Lord says: "This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell; for I have desired it" (Ps 132:14).

3.11.2.en: * The Lord God is not in need; He does not seek a reward, but honor. He does not ask you to return to Him anything from your own. He asks for the firstfruits and the tithes, and will you refuse? This indeed happened when the harvest became meager because of drought of rain, and when hail struck your vineyards and frost destroyed them. Why did this happen but because of your greedy reckonings? He took nine-tenths from you, because you refused to pay the tithes... You will give to the wicked soldier (through captivity or the violence he practices) what you refuse to give to the priest... God is always ready to bestow good things, but the evil of humanity prevents it, because man wants to receive everything from the Lord God, and does not want to offer anything of what he thinks he owns. Now imagine that God says: "Of course you are mine, O man, for I created you. The land you till and the seeds you sow are mine. The animals you use are mine, and also the rain and the breaths of the winds and the heat of the sun are mine. Since all the elements of life are mine, and you have only laid your hands on them, you deserve merely the tithes." Now although Almighty God in His tenderness feeds us, and gives man an abundant reward for his small labor, He demands the tithes for Himself and leaves all the rest to us.

3.12.0.en: 13 "Your words have been stout against me, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee? 14 Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts? 15 And now we call the proud happy; yea, they that work wickedness are set up; yea, they that tempt God are even delivered."

3.12.1.en: Your words have been stout against me, saith the LORD.

3.12.2.en: Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee? [13]

3.12.3.en: As the people were occupied with material wealth, they looked among themselves and saw the wicked rich and the proud occupying positions of leadership, so they counted what they had offered in their worship of offerings and sacrifices as worthless, and perhaps even counted it a loss. They lost what they offered to the Temple and received nothing, but rather trials came upon them and sorrow prevailed among them.

3.12.4.en: Here He presents the eighth accusation, which is that their words have been stout against the Lord, and some translate it as words that are bold against the Lord. In boldness without reverence they spoke against the Lord, and objected to Him, and counted worship of Him a waste of time and money, and an entry into a state of sorrow and bitterness.

3.12.5.en: They denied what they had said, whether openly or secretly, with their mouths or with their minds and thoughts. "What have we spoken against thee?" They asked the prophet to produce proof of this accusation directed against them. Perhaps here they do not deny what they said, but they counted it a trifling matter not worthy of the prophet's uproar against them. As though they were saying: What we said is counted as nothing compared with what the pagan nations said against the Lord, and the evils we practiced are counted as nothing compared with the evils of the nations, so why all this uproar?

3.12.6.en: They did not endure the words of rebuke, and instead of looking into their depths, to ask the Lord to cleanse and sanctify them, they compared themselves with other nations and counted themselves righteous and good. For this reason the Apostle Paul asks us to compare spiritual things with spiritual (1 Cor 2:13).

3.12.7.en: Ye have said, It is vain to serve God.

3.13.0.en: And what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts? [14]

3.13.1.en: And now we call the proud happy; yea, they that work wickedness are set up.

3.14.0.en: Yea, they that tempt God are even delivered. [15]

3.14.1.en: As they compared themselves with the pagan nations, they counted worship of God vain, since it brought them to sorrow, while the proud pagans who refuse to believe in the living God, and the workers of evil, live in surpassing happiness, building and growing and lacking nothing. They call the wicked blessed and regret their clinging to the Lord and worshiping Him, as though He were a source of sorrow and gloom.

3.14.2.en: These did not realize that the cause of their sorrow and unhappiness is not the worship of God, but that they teach as doctrines the commandments of men (Mt 15:9), and that they draw near to the Lord with their lips while their hearts are far from Him (Mt 15:8). They did not realize that the secret of their misery is their attachment to earthly gifts and temporal comfort. As the Apostle Paul says: "If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable" (1 Cor 15:19). But he who worships the Lord in spirit and with heavenly wisdom realizes that "her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace" (Prov 3:17).
